chapter_title: Event Listening and Real-time Updates in React dApps

screens.title: Event Listening and Real-time Updates
screens.subtitle: Use smart contract events and Web3.js to drive live UI updates in React dApps

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn how smart contract events let your dApp react to on-chain changes without constant polling. Events are compact messages emitted by contracts when something important happens — for example, when stored data changes, an NFT mints, or a token transfers. By subscribing with Web3. js you can receive those events in real time and update React state so the user interface refreshes instantly. Practically, this means less network cost, better UX, and fewer stale views. We'll cover methods you actually use: the myContract. events. MyEvent pattern for live subscriptions, getPastEvents for historical data to build initial lists, and the important cleanup pattern inside useEffect that prevents memory leaks. You will also see how to read event. returnValues to extract the emitted parameters and use them as trusted inputs for your UI. The hands-on sequence modifies a SimpleStorage contract to emit DataChanged and updates a custom hook so storedData updates automatically when events arrive. By the end you'll be able to design a reliable listener, handle errors, and test updates from a separate wallet. Think about when polling might still be necessary and how events complement it.

keyIdea.title: Why events matter
keyIdea.text: Events provide efficient, real-time signals from contracts to your dApp. They reduce polling, improve UX, and let React update state the moment a change is mined.

screens.title: Smart Contract Events — Definition and Role
screens.subtitle: What events are, how contracts emit them, and why they appear in dApps

narration.text: A smart contract event is a structured message emitted by a contract when a state-changing action occurs. Events are part of the contract ABI and are written in Solidity with event declarations and emit statements. They are stored in transaction logs on chain and are inexpensive to watch compared to repeated state polling. In practice, your dApp subscribes to these logs through Web3. js, which surfaces an event object containing metadata such as the block number, transaction hash, and a returnValues object that maps parameter names to the emitted values. For example, if you add event DataChanged(address indexed changer, string oldData, string newData) and emit it when setData runs, Web3 delivers that event to subscribers with returnValues. newData. A common misconception is to treat events as authoritative storage; events are logs and not a substitute for reading contract state directly, so use them to trigger UI refreshes or append to lists but validate against contract reads when you require final authority. Key takeaway: events are signals that let your UI react efficiently — design handlers that read useful fields from returnValues and then confirm state if needed.

keyIdea.title: Events are on-chain signals
keyIdea.text: Events are emitted logs that signal contract activity; use them to trigger UI updates and assemble historical lists.

content.html:
Core Concept
Smart Contract Events
Events are logs emitted by contracts to signal that something happened. They are efficient triggers for UI updates.
What an event provides
  • Parameter values in event.returnValues keyed by the Solidity names.
  • Metadata: transactionHash and blockNumber for verification.
  • Indexed parameters support efficient filtering on the node side.
Analogy
Think of events as published messages: the contract publishes a message, subscribers receive it and decide what to do next.
Key Takeaway

Events are excellent for signaling state changes, but confirm critical state by reading contract methods as needed.

Example: Solidity declaration
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract SimpleStorage {
  string public storedData;
  event DataChanged(address indexed changer, string oldData, string newData);

  function setData(string memory newData) public {
    string memory _oldData = storedData;
    storedData = newData;
    emit DataChanged(msg.sender, _oldData, newData);
  }
}
Concrete example
When setData runs, DataChanged emits the old and new values. A dApp watching this event can set storedData from the event immediately.
Common mistake
Relying solely on events as the single source of truth — use them to trigger reads when you need final state verification.

screens.title: Subscribing with myContract.events and handling callbacks
screens.subtitle: How to attach data and error handlers to a live subscription

narration.text: Subscribing to a contract event with Web3. js uses the myContract. events A P I. When you call myContract. events. MyEvent(), Web3 returns an object that allows you to register handlers with. on('data', handler) and. on('error', handler). The data handler receives an event object with returnValues and metadata. A typical pattern is to update local React state inside the data handler and log errors in the error handler. Remember that calling. on returns a subscription you can call unsubscribe on later. A concrete example: simpleStorageContract. events. DataChanged(). on('data', event => setStoredData(event. returnValues. newData)). on('error', err => setError('Error listening')). A common misconception is to assume the data handler only fires for transactions originating from the current UI; in fact it fires for any matching event on chain, including those from other wallets or nodes. That behavior is useful for real-time feeds. When you write handlers, make them idempotent and safe against duplicate deliveries, and consider debouncing UI updates if events arrive in bursts. Closing question: how would you make the handler robust if returnValues might be missing a field? Subscribing with myContract.events and handling callbacks means mycontract.events.eventname() returns a subscription. attach .on('data') to update ui and .on('error') to handle problems; keep the handler idempotent.. In practical terms, how to attach data and error handlers to a live subscription. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Subscription shape
keyIdea.text: myContract.events.EventName() returns a subscription. Attach .on('data') to update UI and .on('error') to handle problems; keep the handler idempotent.

content.html:
Process
Subscribe and attach handlers
The data callback receives the event object; update state with values from returnValues.

const subscription = simpleStorageContract.events.DataChanged()
  .on('data', event => {
    console.log('DataChanged', event);
    setStoredData(event.returnValues.newData);
  })
  .on('error', error => {
    console.error('Event error', error);
  });
Example
A DataChanged event emitted by any transaction will be delivered and can update the primary dApp's storedData immediately.
Pro tip
Make handlers idempotent and guard against undefined returnValues before updating state to avoid errors on malformed events.
Supporting explanation
  • event.returnValues maps parameter names to values emitted by emit.
  • .on('data') receives events from current and past blocks depending on subscription options.
  • .on('error') captures transport or decoding errors and should update user-facing diagnostics.
Key Takeaway

Use the subscription object to manage lifetime and ensure your UI only updates when returnValues are validated.

screens.title: getPastEvents vs live subscriptions
screens.subtitle: When to fetch historical logs and when to subscribe live

narration.text: There are two complementary ways to work with events: fetching past events to build an initial state and subscribing to live events to keep that state updated. getPastEvents('MyEvent', { fromBlock: 0, toBlock: 'latest' }) returns historical logs you can process once at load time to populate lists, while myContract. events. MyEvent() gives you a live feed of new logs as they are mined. Use getPastEvents during initialization to construct a full picture, for example building an NFT list from all past Transfer or Mint events. Then open a live subscription so newly minted items append to the list without reloading. A common misconception is to use only subscriptions and expect historical events to be delivered — live subscriptions typically only deliver events from the moment you subscribe onward unless configured otherwise. Also be mindful of fromBlock range to avoid processing massive logs in the client; paginate or use a backend indexer for very large histories. Practically, combine getPastEvents for initial population and a subscription for incremental updates to achieve both completeness and responsiveness. getPastEvents vs live subscriptions means populate initial state with getpastevents and then keep it fresh with a live mycontract.events subscription.. In practical terms, when to fetch historical logs and when to subscribe live. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Two-step pattern
keyIdea.text: Populate initial state with getPastEvents and then keep it fresh with a live myContract.events subscription.

content.html:
Comparison
getPastEvents
Fetch historical events to build initial lists or to audit past activity.
const past = await myContract.getPastEvents('DataChanged', { fromBlock: 0, toBlock: 'latest' });
past.forEach(e => process(e.returnValues));
Notes:
  • Good for initial population and rebuilding UI state.
  • Can be expensive; restrict block range or paginate.
Comparison
Live Subscriptions
Receive new events as they are mined and update UI in real time without polling.
const sub = myContract.events.DataChanged()
  .on('data', e => handle(e.returnValues))
  .on('error', err => console.error(err));
Notes:
  • Good for low-latency UI updates and feeds.
  • Remember to unsubscribe in cleanup to avoid duplicated handlers.
Key Takeaway

Use getPastEvents for a complete starting picture and a live subscription to receive incremental updates. Combining both gives a robust, responsive dApp experience while controlling cost and complexity.

screens.title: Integrating event listeners in React with useEffect
screens.subtitle: Set up, update state, and clean up subscriptions safely

narration.text: In React, event subscriptions belong in a useEffect so they follow the component lifecycle. The typical pattern checks for the contract instance, sets up the subscription, registers data and error handlers, and returns a cleanup function that calls subscription. unsubscribe(). Doing this prevents memory leaks and duplicated listeners when the component re-renders or the contract instance changes. For example, inside useEffect you might log that you're setting up a listener, then call simpleStorageContract. events. DataChanged(). on('data', event => setStoredData(event. returnValues. newData)). Keep fetchContractData or other dependent functions in the dependency array so the effect updates when they change. A common pitfall is to forget to check that subscription exists before calling unsubscribe in cleanup; guard calls with if (subscription && subscription. unsubscribe) subscription. unsubscribe(). Another pitfall is including unstable function references in dependencies; wrap helpers in useCallback or move them out of the effect to avoid unnecessary resubscriptions. The core idea is: subscribe on mount, update state in handler, and unsubscribe on unmount or when dependencies change. Integrating event listeners in React with useEffect means create subscriptions inside useeffect and return a cleanup that unsubscribes to maintain predictable listener lifetimes.. In practical terms, set up, update state, and clean up subscriptions safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: useEffect lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Create subscriptions inside useEffect and return a cleanup that unsubscribes to maintain predictable listener lifetimes.

content.html:
Process Flow
useEffect subscription pattern
Check contract instance and dependencies before subscribing to avoid runtime errors.
Attach .on('data') to update state, and .on('error') to handle problems gracefully.
Return cleanup that calls subscription.unsubscribe() to remove the listener on unmount or dependency change.
Pitfall
If your effect re-runs frequently due to unstable dependencies, you may create multiple subscriptions. Stabilize dependencies with useCallback or refs.
Concrete snippet
useEffect(() => {
  if (simpleStorageContract) {
    const subscription = simpleStorageContract.events.DataChanged()
      .on('data', event => setStoredData(event.returnValues.newData))
      .on('error', err => console.error(err));

    return () => {
      if (subscription && subscription.unsubscribe) subscription.unsubscribe();
    };
  }
}, [simpleStorageContract]);
Key Takeaway

Place subscriptions in useEffect, stabilize dependencies, and always unsubscribe in the cleanup to keep listeners predictable.

screens.title: Processing event.returnValues
screens.subtitle: Extract parameter values and update UI safely

narration.text: When an event arrives, the returned event object includes returnValues — a keyed object whose keys match the parameter names used in the Solidity emit. For example with event DataChanged(address changer, string oldData, string newData) you access event. returnValues. newData. Use those keys directly in your handler to map emitted data into state. Always validate that the field exists and has the expected type before using it in rendering logic. A concrete example: setStoredData(event. returnValues. newData) will immediately update the string shown on screen. If your event includes indexed parameters, you can also use filters on subscription creation to limit noise. A subtle misconception to avoid is assuming returnValues always includes the same shape; if the contract ABI or emitted parameters change, handlers must be updated accordingly. For arrays or nested data emitted as tuples, parse and map each element before storing. After processing returnValues, you may optionally trigger a targeted re-fetch of contract state to ensure consistency for critical flows. Final question: how would you handle a missing returnValues. newData in a production handler? Processing event.returnValues means use the solidity parameter names to extract fields from event.returnvalues and validate them before updating state.. In practical terms, extract parameter values and update ui safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: returnValues mapping
keyIdea.text: Use the Solidity parameter names to extract fields from event.returnValues and validate them before updating state.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Read returnValues safely
Use the names from Solidity's emit and guard for presence and type.
.on('data', event => {
  // Example safe access
  const newData = event && event.returnValues && event.returnValues.newData;
  if (typeof newData === 'string') {
    setStoredData(newData);
  } else {
    console.warn('Unexpected event shape', event);
  }
});
Example
When newData arrives as a string, update state directly. If missing, log and optionally re-fetch from the contract.
Supporting notes
  • Names in returnValues match the Solidity emit parameter names.
  • Indexed params are useful for filters but still appear inside returnValues.
  • For critical flows, validate and re-read the contract state after using the event value.
Common mistake
Assuming events always arrive in order; block reorgs or node behavior can reorder or re-emit events in rare cases—design handlers that tolerate minor inconsistencies.

screens.title: Modifying SimpleStorage to emit DataChanged
screens.subtitle: Solidity change to support event-driven UI updates

narration.text: The first practical step is to modify your SimpleStorage contract to emit an event when setData runs. The provided code declares event DataChanged(address indexed changer, string oldData, string newData) and emits it after updating storedData. This pattern is straightforward: capture the old value to include in the event, update the state variable, and then emit the event with msg. sender so listeners know who made the change. After you recompile and redeploy the contract, update your frontend ABI and contract address so Web3 can decode incoming events correctly. A common oversight is forgetting to update the ABI or address, which makes event decoding fail or produce undefined returnValues. Also remember to add indexed to parameters that you want to filter on, like the address of the changer. Once deployed, the event gives your dApp the signal it needs to update storedData in real time without polling the contract method. Modifying SimpleStorage to emit DataChanged means emit datachanged in setdata with old and new values plus msg.sender so listeners can update ui and attribute changes.. In practical terms, solidity change to support event-driven ui updates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Emit on write
keyIdea.text: Emit DataChanged in setData with old and new values plus msg.sender so listeners can update UI and attribute changes.

content.html:
Hands-on
Add DataChanged to SimpleStorage
Recompile, redeploy, and update your frontend ABI and address after making the change.
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract SimpleStorage {
  string public storedData;
  event DataChanged(address indexed changer, string oldData, string newData);

  constructor(string memory initialData) {
    storedData = initialData;
  }

  function setData(string memory newData) public {
    string memory _oldData = storedData;
    storedData = newData;
    emit DataChanged(msg.sender, _oldData, newData);
  }
}
Practical checklist
  • Recompile and redeploy the contract after changing events.
  • Update src/contracts/SimpleStorage.json ABI and VITE_SIMPLE_STORAGE_CONTRACT_ADDRESS in your .env.
  • Verify the event is present using getPastEvents or by sending a test transaction.
Key Takeaway

Emit an event whenever a meaningful write occurs so clients can react without polling the chain.

screens.title: Enhancing useSimpleStorage hook with an event listener
screens.subtitle: Wire simpleStorageContract.events.DataChanged into your hook and update state

The pattern shown in the source uses useEffect: after ensuring simpleStorageContract exists, create the subscription with simpleStorageContract. events. DataChanged(). Attach a data handler that calls setStoredData(event. returnValues. newData) and an error handler that sets an error state. Crucially, return a cleanup function that calls subscription. unsubscribe() if available. This prevents listeners from persisting after the hook consumer unmounts or the contract instance changes. When integrating into your app, you don't need to change App. jsx; the storedData state exposed by the hook will update automatically and components will re-render. A common testing approach is to open two browser windows, call setData from one, and observe the primary dApp update in the other, confirming the event flow. Remember to stabilize fetchContractData or other functions with useCallback if they appear in the dependency array to avoid repeated subscriptions. Enhancing useSimpleStorage hook with an event listener means add the datachanged subscription inside the hook's useeffect so storeddata updates across components without additional wiring.. In practical terms, wire simplestoragecontract.events.datachanged into your hook and update state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. keyIdea.title: Hook-level subscription
keyIdea.text: Add the DataChanged subscription inside the hook's useEffect so storedData updates across components without additional wiring.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
useSimpleStorage: add subscription
useEffect(() => {
  if (simpleStorageContract) {
    const subscription = simpleStorageContract.events.DataChanged()
      .on('data', event => {
        setStoredData(event.returnValues.newData);
      })
      .on('error', error => {
        setError('Error listening to contract events.');
      });

    return () => {
      if (subscription && subscription.unsubscribe) {
        subscription.unsubscribe();
      }
    };
  }
}, [simpleStorageContract]);
Notes: place this inside the same hook that manages storedData so any consumer benefits automatically.
Testing tip
Open a second browser and a different wallet. Trigger setData from the other wallet and verify the primary UI updates without refresh. This proves cross-client event delivery.
Common mistake
Forgetting to update the hook's dependencies or leaving unstable callbacks in the array leads to repeated subscriptions. Stabilize functions with useCallback.

screens.title: Subscription ownership and architecture choices
screens.subtitle: Decide where to create subscriptions: hook, component, or backend

narration.text: Deciding where to place event subscriptions affects maintainability and performance. You can create the subscription in a per-component useEffect when only that component needs the events. Alternatively, create the subscription centrally inside a hook (like useSimpleStorage) so multiple components share the same state and you avoid duplicate listeners. For larger apps, consider a backend or WebSocket relay that indexes events and serves them to clients; this offloads heavy historical queries and supports pagination. The chapter's recommended pattern is a hook-level subscription because it centralizes logic, keeps UI simple, and makes cleanup straightforward. Watch for a misconception: centralizing subscriptions is useful, but centralization without careful lifecycle management can still create leaks if the hook recreates subscriptions frequently. Use stable contract instances, memoize helpers, and manage unsubscribe calls carefully. Use getPastEvents on initial load where you need completeness and rely on subscriptions only for incremental updates. The architecture you choose depends on scale: small dApps benefit from hook-level subscriptions, while production-scale feeds often need an indexing backend. Subscription ownership and architecture choices means prefer hook-level subscriptions for shared state; move to an indexed backend when you need pagination or heavy history queries.. In practical terms, decide where to create subscriptions: hook, component, or backend. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Where to subscribe
keyIdea.text: Prefer hook-level subscriptions for shared state; move to an indexed backend when you need pagination or heavy history queries.

content.html:
Architecture
Where to create subscriptions
Choose the subscription owner based on reuse and scale requirements.
Component-level
Good for one-off listeners, but risks duplicate listeners if multiple components mount.
Hook-level
Centralizes logic; a single hook can expose state to many components and manage a single subscription and cleanup.
Backend indexer
Best for large histories, pagination, and advanced queries. Relays events to clients over websockets or APIs.
Key Takeaway

For most dApps, a hook-level subscription balances simplicity and reuse. Move to indexed backends only when history or scale demands it.

screens.title: Error handling, filters, and idempotence
screens.subtitle: Make listeners robust in real-world networks

narration.text: Robust event listeners need error handling, optional filtering, and idempotent state updates. Attach an. on('error') handler that logs and surfaces a user-friendly message or sets an error state. Use filters in the subscription like myContract. events. Transfer({ filter: { to: contractAddress } }) to reduce event noise at the node level. When events can be re-emitted due to reconnections or rare chain reorgs, design handlers that detect duplicates — for example by checking transactionHash plus log index or by maintaining a set of processed event IDs in memory. Idempotence ensures applying the same event twice doesn't corrupt state. Another important practice is guarding unsubscribe calls in cleanup to avoid exceptions if the subscription object lacks unsubscribe. Finally, avoid updating deeply nested state directly from events without validation; consider transforming and sanitizing returned fields before storing and rendering. These practices make your listeners resilient to network blips and node differences. Error handling, filters, and idempotence means add error handlers, use filters to limit traffic, ensure idempotent updates, and validate before applying event data.. In practical terms, make listeners robust in real-world networks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Robust listeners
keyIdea.text: Add error handlers, use filters to limit traffic, ensure idempotent updates, and validate before applying event data.

content.html:
Best Practice
Error handling & filters
Use .on('error') to capture transport issues and apply filters to subscriptions to reduce noise.
Example filter:
myContract.events.Transfer({ filter: { to: contractAddress } })
  .on('data', handler)
  .on('error', err => console.error(err));
Idempotence
Track processed events by transactionHash+logIndex or keep a Set of seen IDs so repeating the same event does not duplicate entries.
Common mistake
Not sanitizing event data from returnValues before applying it to state can lead to rendering errors or injection of unexpected types.
Key Takeaway

Design handlers to tolerate duplicates, network errors, and missing fields. Filters and validation keep listeners efficient and safe.
